title: Net domestic product
gist: FRED Blog explains net domestic product as GDP minus consumption of fixed capital, filtering out replacement investment; in the US the two series track closely, though quarterly growth rates can differ by up to half a percentage point.

insights.claim: Net domestic product equals GDP minus the consumption of fixed capital, so it counts only production that is not replacing depreciated capital.
insights.so_what: NDP is a cleaner gauge of net new output when investment is distorted by replacement spending.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog

insights.claim: After a disaster such as a hurricane, rebuilding lifts investment and GDP although it only replaces broken capital, so an economy can look strong without adding net output.
insights.so_what: Post-disaster GDP rebounds overstate real expansion.
insights.locator: But say that a country is hit by a major hurricane
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog

insights.claim: Real GDP and real NDP track each other closely for the US because the economy is large and diversified, but quarterly growth rates differ by up to half a percentage point, sometimes with GDP growing more and sometimes NDP.
insights.so_what: Differences are small but not negligible; useful as a cross-check on GDP quality.
insights.locator: But if you look into the details
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
